newsitem.title: Australia: Aboriginal boys out of jail after attack on MP.
newsitem.headline: Aboriginal boys out of jail after attack on MP.

text.p: Two Aboriginal boys jailed for spitting at Australian race row politician Pauline Hanson were granted bail on Monday at a special children's court hearing but were told they could not go home for Christmas.
The two brothers, aged 11 and 12, were granted bail as long as they remained in a rural training centre for wayward Aboriginal children.
In a special hearing in the Brisbane Children's Court the boys, who were last week remanded without bail until January 30, were told they would not be allowed home.
Judge Fred McGuire called instead for the boys to spend Wednesday's Christmas festival at the camp with their families.
Human rights watchdog Amnesty International on Monday warned that Australia may have breached the U.N. child rights covenant by jailing the two boys.
"Amnesty International is not condoning what these boys allegedly did," said Heinz Schurmann-Zeggel, acting director for Amnesty in the Asia-Pacific region.

"But we are appalled that they could be remanded in custody for it, even for more than one day, let alone across Christmas or until the end of January," Schurmann-Zeggel told Australian radio from London.
"Amnesty International is concerned that in this context it seems Australia might have been in violation of international obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child."
Last Thursday the two Aboriginal boys were remanded in custody pending a trial after being charged with aggravated assault and unlawful assembly.
The boys were part of a group of four boys who entered Hanson's electoral office in the Queensland town of Ipswich on Wednesday on the pretence of seeking her autograph.

But after speaking to Hanson briefly, the boys spat on Hanson and slapped her in the face, according to evidence in their brief court appearance. Three of them were charged, one of whom was released on bail.
Aboriginal groups have reacted angrily to the jailing and Queensland's senior lawmaker, Attorney General Denver Beanland, said he would review the original court ruling.

Independent politician Hanson sparked a divisive race debate in September when she delivered her maiden parliamentary speech, claiming Asians were swamping Australia and that disadvantaged Aborigines were given unfair governmnent assistance.
The continuing race debate has sparked a record number of racial discrimination complaints
There are about 300,000 Aborigines in Australia's 18 million population. Aborigines have a life expectancy 10-15 years shorter than non-indigenous Australians.

A report last week said young Aboriginals were more than 20 times more likely to be held in juvenile detention centres than non-indigenous children. In conservative Queensland state they were 41 times more likely to be held.
